title: Three Years and Over 100 No's Before Canva's First Investment
dek: From a Perth living room, Melanie Perkins and Cliff Obrecht pitched a simple design tool to investors who kept saying no, and rewrote the pitch each time.

story.event: Being turned down by more than 100 investors between 2010 and 2013 before raising Canva's seed round
story.summary: After meeting the Silicon Valley investor Bill Tai at a Perth conference in 2010, Melanie Perkins and Cliff Obrecht, who ran the yearbook business Fusion Books, spent about three years pitching a simple online design tool; a first trip to San Francisco produced no investors, and more than 100 turned them down. They refined the pitch after each rejection, recruited Cameron Adams as a third co-founder in 2012, and in March 2013 announced a $3 million seed round that included a Commercialisation Australia grant; Canva opened to users in August 2013.
paragraphs: In 2010, at a conference in Perth, Melanie Perkins described her idea to Bill Tai, a visiting Silicon Valley investor. He was on his phone while she talked, and she took that to mean he was not interested. "But then I got home and realized that he was actually introducing me to a few people," she later told CNBC.

Since 2007 she and her boyfriend, Cliff Obrecht, had run Fusion Books, an online tool for designing school yearbooks, from her mother's living room. It worked; by 2013 more than a tenth of Australian high schools used it. They saw it as a test of something larger, a simple design tool on the web for anyone, which grew from her years tutoring students who needed a semester to find the buttons in professional software. That needed investors, and, she said, "At the start we didn't know what venture capital was."

Tai's introductions led to San Francisco, where her first fundraising trip brought three months of rejection. "We came back without a single investor," she said in 2024. Over the following years more than 100 investors turned them down, and many US investors, she found, wanted only US-based companies. Tai urged them to join his kitesurfing retreats, and she took up a sport she said she would not normally have tried. After each no they reworked the pitch. Early decks opened with the product; later ones spent most of their slides on the problem and how many people it touched. Through Lars Rasmussen, a co-founder of Google Maps and their adviser, they met Cameron Adams, a former Google designer, who first said no and then joined as a third co-founder in 2012.

Canva was founded that August. In March 2013 it announced a $3 million seed round from investors including Tai, Rasmussen, Matrix Partners, 500 Startups and Blackbird Ventures, with a government Commercialisation Australia grant that she said helped them stay in Australia. "There were three years between meeting our first investor and actually landing an investment," she recalled. Canva opened to its first users on 26 August 2013. Of those years she later said, "I had to come to terms with the idea that if things didn't work out I wouldn't hate myself."

quote.text: His skill is the same in each case, but he is distracted by the value of his stake. And every one who attaches importance to the external, becomes internally without resource.
quote.locator: Chapter XIX, "The Secret of Life" (Confucius on the gambler and the stake)
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Zhuangzi's gambler plays well for counters and loses his wits when he stakes gold. Perkins staked years on money other people held, and Zhuangzi would warn that so much weight on the external empties a person within. Her private settlement with failure may be an answer to him, or may not.

reflection: The part of this story usually retold is that Perkins would not give up. The quieter parts are what she did with each no, moving the problem to the front of the pitch and the product further back, and the private settlement she made with herself about failing.

Zhuangzi would say that settlement is part of the skill, not a retreat from it. When everything rides on one meeting, you hear less of what is said in it. If you describe talQen to someone this week, try leading with the problem they live with, and go in having already forgiven yourself if the answer is no.
invitation: Write one sentence describing the problem your work solves, in the words of the person who has it, without naming your product. Keep it somewhere you will see it before your next conversation about the work.

cross_checks.claim: Perkins met Bill Tai at a conference in Perth around 2010, and he introduced her to other investors
More than 100 investors turned Perkins down before Canva's seed round
She refined the pitch deck after each rejection
Lars Rasmussen's introduction brought Cameron Adams in as a co-founder in 2012
Canva raised a $3 million seed round in early 2013 that included Commercialisation Australia funding
Canva opened to users on 26 August 2013

research_notes: Seed money: SmartCompany (March 2013) reports a $3 million seed round to which Commercialisation Australia contributed through a programme offering up to $2 million; CNBC (2020) describes an initial $1.5 million round matched by the Australian government; Women's Agenda (2024) reports $3 million from investors and, separately, a $2 million Commercialisation Australia seed investment. The story uses the contemporary $3 million figure 'with a Commercialisation Australia grant' and gives no grant amount. First-year users: Women's Agenda says 600,000 in the first twelve months, Gulf News 150,000 active users in the first year; the story uses neither. Timing: SmartCompany (2013) says the round took almost a year, while Perkins in 2016 said three years passed between meeting her first investor and landing an investment; both are consistent with meeting Tai in 2010 and closing in early 2013, and the story quotes her three years. The figure of more than 100 rejections is Perkins's own account, repeated in SmartCompany (2016), Gulf News and elsewhere; no source lists the investors. Sources differ on where the pitching happened (Perth, San Francisco, both); the story mentions only San Francisco for the first trip, as she described it. SmartCompany said in March 2013 that Canva would launch in May; it opened on 26 August 2013. Bill Tai is described as a lead seed investor by Women's Agenda and as one investor among several by SmartCompany; the story lists him among the investors. The Zhuangzi passage is Confucius's explanation to Yen Yuan of a boatman's skill; it begins after a translator's footnote on the gambler's girdle.
